claim: Snap moved more than 2 exabytes of data (roughly 1.5 trillion media files) from Amazon S3 Standard-IA to Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, and as a result saved tens of millions of dollars on storage.
question: What did Snap gain by moving saved media from S3 Standard-IA to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval?

values.display: saved tens of millions of dollars on storage

evidence.quote: Snap migrated more than 2 exabytes of data—roughly equivalent to 1.5 trillion media files—seamlessly to Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval from Amazon S3 Standard-IA.
As a result of the migration, the company saved tens of millions of dollars on storage.

claim: Snap first analyzed the access patterns of its data; the analysis showed that S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval would reduce costs because the class is ideal for data that needs immediate access but is accessed only once per quarter. Snap then migrated with S3 Lifecycle policies.
question: How did Snap decide that S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval was cheaper than S3 Standard-IA for its saved media?

values.display: needs immediate access but is only accessed once per quarter

evidence.quote: This analysis showed that using Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval would reduce costs because the storage class is ideal for data that needs immediate access but is only accessed once per quarter.
So, Snap began migrating to the storage class in March 2022 using Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies.

claim: Bynder stores 18 PB of customer data, more than 175 million assets, in S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which has led to a storage cost saving of 65 percent.
question: What did Bynder save by storing its digital assets in S3 Intelligent-Tiering?

evidence.quote: Now, 18 PB of Bynder’s customer data—equating to more than 175 million assets—is stored using S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which has led to a storage cost savings of 65 percent.

claim: Bynder chose S3 Intelligent-Tiering because its data access patterns change often, which makes traditional storage options less cost effective; the class reviews the access pattern of assets automatically instead of by hand.
question: Why did Bynder pick S3 Intelligent-Tiering over a fixed storage class?

evidence.quote: Bynder’s data access patterns frequently change, which makes traditional storage options less cost effective.
Instead of having to manually review the access pattern of assets, S3 Intelligent-Tiering does it for us automatically.

claim: Bynder puts tags on each S3 bucket and uses AWS Cost Explorer so that it can track S3 storage costs per product offering.
question: How does Bynder track its S3 storage cost per product?

values.display: allocates tags to each Amazon S3 bucket

evidence.quote: The company allocates tags to each Amazon S3 bucket so that it can carefully track costs and adjust as needed.
To further reduce its expenses, Bynder adopted AWS Cost Explorer, a service to visualize, understand, and manage AWS costs and usage over time.

claim: When customers are in two geographic locations, Cross-Region Replication can minimize latency by keeping object copies in AWS Regions that are geographically closer to the users.
question: When does Cross-Region Replication help latency rather than compliance?

evidence.quote: If your customers are in two geographic locations, you can minimize latency in accessing objects by maintaining object copies in AWS Regions that are geographically closer to your users.

claim: If compute clusters in two different AWS Regions analyze the same set of objects, Cross-Region Replication can keep object copies in both Regions for operational efficiency.
question: Why replicate data to a second Region that runs its own analytics cluster?

evidence.quote: **Increase operational efficiency** – If you have compute clusters in two different AWS Regions that analyze the same set of objects, you might choose to maintain object copies in those Regions.

claim: Replication can put replicas directly into S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive or another storage class in the destination bucket; or it can keep the same class and let a lifecycle configuration on the destination move replicas to a colder class as they age.
question: Can a replica be stored in a cheaper storage class than its source object?

values.display: directly put objects into S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive, or another storage class

evidence.quote: You can use replication to directly put objects into S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive, or another storage class in the destination buckets. You can also replicate your data to the same storage class and use lifecycle configurations on the destination buckets to move your objects to a colder storage class as they age.

claim: With the owner override option, replication changes replica ownership to the AWS account that owns the destination bucket, whoever owns the source object; this can be used to restrict access to the replicas.
question: How can a replica in another account be owned by that account instead of the source owner?

evidence.quote: Regardless of who owns the source object, you can tell Amazon S3 to change replica ownership to the AWS account that owns the destination bucket. This is referred to as the *owner override* option. You can use this option to restrict access to object replicas.

claim: To fail over to a bucket in another Region and keep all metadata and objects in sync, set up two-way (bi-directional) replication rules before configuring Multi-Region Access Point failover controls, so data written to the failover bucket is replicated back to the source bucket.
question: What must be in place before Multi-Region Access Point failover so that no writes are lost on failback?

qualifiers.scope: S3 Replication with Multi-Region Access Points
qualifiers.condition: failover with Multi-Region Access Point failover controls

evidence.quote: To keep all metadata and objects in sync across buckets during data replication, use two-way replication (also known as bi-directional replication) rules before configuring Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Point failover controls. Two-way replication rules help ensure that when data is written to the S3 bucket that traffic fails over to, that data is then replicated back to the source bucket.

claim: An Object Lock retention period can be set uniquely for individual objects, and a default retention period can also be set on the bucket.
question: Can Object Lock retention differ between objects in the same bucket?

values.display: a unique retention period for individual objects
a default retention period on an S3 bucket

evidence.quote: You can set a unique retention period for individual objects. Additionally, you can set a default retention period on an S3 bucket.

claim: A bucket policy can restrict the minimum and maximum allowed Object Lock retention periods with the s3:object-lock-remaining-retention-days condition key.
question: How do you stop users from setting too short or too long an Object Lock retention period?

qualifiers.scope: bucket policy on an Object Lock bucket

evidence.quote: You may also restrict the minimum and maximum allowable retention periods with the `s3:object-lock-remaining-retention-days` condition key in the bucket policy.

claim: A bucket policy can grant another account cross-account permission to upload objects while ensuring that the bucket owner has full control of the uploaded objects.
question: Which policy type lets another account upload into your bucket while you keep full control of the objects?

values.display: grants cross-account permissions to upload objects

evidence.quote: For example, you can create a bucket policy that grants cross-account permissions to upload objects to an S3 bucket while ensuring that the bucket owner has full control of the uploaded objects.

claim: A bucket policy can use wildcard characters in ARNs and other values to grant permissions to a subset of objects, such as objects that begin with a common prefix or end with a given extension.
question: How can one bucket policy grant access to only one prefix or file type?

values.display: wildcard characters on Amazon Resource Names (ARNs)

evidence.quote: In your bucket policy, you can use wildcard characters on Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) and other values to grant permissions to a subset of objects.

claim: When the bucket owner and the parent account of the user are the same account, the bucket owner can grant access with either a bucket policy or a user policy.
question: In a single account, must S3 access be granted with a bucket policy?

values.display: either a bucket policy or a user policy

qualifiers.condition: bucket owner and the user's parent account are the same

evidence.quote: In the following scenario, the bucket owner and the parent account to which the user belongs are the same. So the bucket owner can use either a bucket policy or a user policy to grant access.

claim: An account that owns an S3 resource can grant permissions to another AWS account, which can then delegate them (or a subset) to its own users; but an account that received permissions from another account cannot delegate them cross-account to a further AWS account.
question: Can an account that was granted access to a bucket pass that access on to a third account?

values.display: can't delegate permission cross-account to another AWS account

evidence.quote: If an AWS account owns a resource, it can grant those permissions to another AWS account. That account can then delegate those permissions, or a subset of them, to users in the account. This is referred to as* permission delegation*. But an account that receives permissions from another account can't delegate permission cross-account to another AWS account.
